1.title: Hackers use an old Apple flaw
1.text: A US agency named CISA has a new warning. Hackers are using an old flaw in Apple devices. Apple fixed it in May 2024. But many people did not update. A Russian spy group may be behind the attacks. They use websites to steal data from phones and computers. Update your Apple devices now.

2.title: CISA warns about an old Apple flaw used by hackers
2.text:
The US agency CISA added an Apple flaw to its list of known exploited problems. It is called CVE-2024-27834. Apple fixed it in May 2024, and it was first shown at a hacking contest in March of that year. But hackers are using it now.

The security company Sekoia says a hacking group linked to Russia, called APT29, is behind the attacks. Sekoia is fairly sure of this. The group uses real websites that were hacked, fake websites, and an attack on a tool named Plerdy SEO Tracker. A bad script checks the visitor's device and then steals browser data, such as cookies. US government agencies must fix their devices by November 18, 2026.

3.title: CISA says hackers are exploiting a patched Apple flaw to steal data
3.text:
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added a medium-severity Apple flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after reports of active attacks. The flaw, CVE-2024-27834, has a score of 5.5 and lets an attacker who can already read and write memory bypass Pointer Authentication. Apple fixed it in May 2024 in iOS, macOS, Safari and other products. It was first demonstrated at the Pwn2Own contest in Vancouver in March of that year.

The move follows a report from Sekoia, which says hackers possibly linked to Russia used old, patched flaws in Safari and Google Chrome to deliver malware that collects data from browsers and devices. Sekoia attributes the activity to APT29, also known as Cozy Bear and Midnight Blizzard, a group tied to Russia's foreign intelligence service, with moderate to high confidence.

The attackers reach victims in three ways: hacked legitimate websites, fake sites that copy popular ones, and a supply chain attack on Plerdy SEO Tracker. Malicious JavaScript profiles the visitor's device and then triggers the flaw. The payload steals browser cookies. CISA recommends that federal civilian agencies apply the patches by November 18, 2026.
